Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:

- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Poisoning
sources.text:
Poisoning. Many everyday foods, medicines and plants are toxic. Act fast, even if your pet seems fine. Signs can take hours or days.
Signs: Vomiting, drooling or diarrhea; Shaking, twitching or seizures; Wobbly, unusually sleepy or overexcited; Pale gums, bleeding or bruising (rat poison); Trouble breathing
Common poisons: Chocolate, coffee and energy drinks; Grapes and raisins; Onions, garlic and chives; Xylitol: sugar-free gum, candy and some peanut butters; Human painkillers. Paracetamol is deadly to cats; ibuprofen harms both cats and dogs.; Rat and mouse poison, insect sprays and pesticides; Lilies (cats). Even pollen or the vase water can cause kidney failure.; Dog flea and tick products on cats (permethrin); Alcohol, cleaning products and antifreeze
What to do now:
1. Move your pet away from the source and remove anything left in their mouth, if it's safe to do so.
2. Note what they ate, about how much, and when. Bring the packaging, label or a piece of the plant.
3. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and tell them you're on your way.
4. If it's on their skin or fur (for example a flea product), wash with mild dish soap and lukewarm water, then rinse well.
Don't: Making your pet vomit unless a vet tells you to. It's dangerous with some poisons and if your pet is drowsy. Home remedies like salt, milk, oil or hydrogen peroxide. Giving any human medicine.
Go to a vet now.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: How often should I bathe my Shih Tzu?
A: Most Shih Tzus do well with a bath every 3 to 4 weeks. Bathing too often can dry out their skin.

- Brush before the bath to remove tangles, then dry them fully, especially the ears
- Wipe the eyes and face daily, as tear stains and food build up there

Many owners keep a short "puppy cut" with a groom every 4 to 6 weeks, which makes daily care much easier.

sources.label: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals
sources.text:
Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Overview
There are many health benefits of owning a pet. They can increase opportunities to exercise, get outside, and socialize. Regular walking or playing with pets can decrease blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and triglyceride levels. Pets can help manage loneliness and depression by providing companionship. Studies have shown that the bond between people and their pets is linked to several health benefits, including: - Decreased blood pressure, cholesterol and triglyceride (fat) levels, feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. - Increased opportunities for exercise and outdoor activities, better cognitive function in older adults, and more opportunities to socialize. However, pets can sometimes carry harmful germs that can make us sick even when the pet appears healthy. The diseases people get from animals are called zoonotic diseases. Below are some tips to help you and your family stay healthy while enjoying pets.

sources.label: CDC Healthy Pets, Cats
sources.text:
Cats — Overview
Nearly 40 million households in the United States have pet cats. Research has shown that cats can provide emotional support, improve moods, and contribute to the overall morale of their owners. Cats are also credited with promoting socialization among older people and physically or mentally disabled people. Although cats are great companions, cat owners should be aware that sometimes cats can carry harmful germs that can make people sick. This can happen even when they appear healthy and clean.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: My dog licked toilet bowl cleaner and my cat stepped in spilled bleach. What do I do?
A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners, as this makes a toxic gas.

Q: How much exercise does my old dog need?
A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

Make home easier:
- Non-slip rugs or yoga mats on smooth floors
- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

If your dog limps, stops often or is stiff after walks, he may be in pain. Ask your vet for a check and an exercise plan.

Q: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?
A: No. In cats, open-mouth breathing is a sign of serious trouble and means she may not be getting enough oxygen. Fast or hard breathing, sitting or crouching in a stiff upright position, and bluish gums are also warning signs.

This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

On the way:
- Keep her as calm and still as possible.
- Put her in a carrier or box with good air holes, and cover it lightly with a cloth to help her feel safe.
- Don't hold her tightly or press on her chest.
- Call the clinic ahead so the team can get ready for her.

sources.text: Q: My cat is losing hair. Is it normal shedding? A: Normal shedding thins the coat evenly, with no bald patches. Hair loss is different: bald or thin patches, or hair missing from both sides of the body. Hair loss is a sign of another problem, not a disease on its own. Common causes in cats are fleas and flea allergy (the most common cause of hair loss on both sides), other parasites, fungal or bacterial skin infections, allergies, and overgrooming from stress or pain. See your vet if you notice: - Bald or thin patches, or red, scabby or sore skin - Your cat licking or scratching the same spot a lot - Hair loss that is sudden, spreading or not settling - Hair loss together with weight loss, low energy or a change in eating or drinking Your vet will check for fleas and skin infection, and may run skin, blood or urine tests to find the cause. …

Q: My cat has round bald patches. Is it ringworm?
A: It might be. Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm. It is a fungal skin infection. Signs include:
- Round patches of hair loss
- Broken or stubbly hair
- Scaly, crusty or red skin
- Dandruff or extra grooming

Ringworm spreads to people and other pets, and children are at higher risk. Its spores can stay in a home for many months.

What to do:
- See your vet, since flea allergy and other problems can look similar
- Keep the cat in one easy-to-clean room during treatment
- Wash hands after handling her
- Clean and disinfect the home well

Treatment often takes six weeks or more.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: Lily pollen got on my cat's fur and she drank water from the flower vase. Is she in danger?
A: Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

Q: My old cat drinks a lot of water and pees a lot. Why?
A: Drinking and peeing more is a common early sign of kidney disease in older cats. Kidney disease affects up to 40% of cats over 10 and about 80% of cats over 15.

Other signs can follow:
- Weight loss
- Poor appetite
- Low energy and a messy coat

The same signs can also come from diabetes or an overactive thyroid, so blood and urine tests are needed to find the cause.

Book a vet visit soon, and don't limit her water. Go to a vet today if she stops eating, vomits repeatedly or seems very weak. Catching kidney disease early, often with a special diet, can help your cat feel better for longer.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Cats — Monitor your cat’s health
Take your cat to the veterinarian regularly to keep it healthy and prevent infectious diseases. When sheltering at home with your pet, make sure the room chosen is pet friendly. Select a safe room, preferably an interior room with no (or few) windows. Remove any toxic chemicals or plants. Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

About Cleaning and Disinfecting Pet Supplies — Using bleach solution
- Clean and scrub with soapy water first to remove dirt. - Rinse with water to remove any remaining dirt and soapy water. - Prepare a diluted household bleach solution by mixing 2 oz (1/4 cup) bleach and 1 gallon water. - Disinfect the item by soaking it in the bleach solution for at least 10 minutes. Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Keep children away from areas that might contain dog or cat poop to prevent them from getting roundworms and hookworms. Cover sand boxes so cats don't use them as a litter box.

Q: My cat swallowed one of my paracetamol (Biogesic) tablets that fell on the floor.
A: This is an emergency. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

sources.text:
Q: What does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?
A: The number tells you how many diseases one shot protects against. Combining them means fewer injections.

Labels often use letters, for example:
- D = distemper
- A2 = adenovirus type 2 (protects against hepatitis)
- P = parvovirus
- P = parainfluenza
- L = leptospirosis

So "DA2PP" covers four diseases, and adding L gives "DA2LPP". Products differ in what they add, such as extra lepto strains or other germs, so the number alone doesn't tell you the exact mix.

For cats, the common combo is FVRCP: feline viral rhinotracheitis (herpesvirus), calicivirus and panleukopenia.

Ask your vet which diseases your pet's vaccine card covers.

sources.label: FurFriends checked answer
sources.text:
Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

Q: My dog was panting really hard after our walk in the heat and now he collapsed. What do I do?
A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Tips for handling injured pets
Even the gentlest pet can bite or scratch if injured. Pain and fear can make animals unpredictable or even dangerous. Try to get your pet to a veterinarian as quickly as possible without risking injury or illness to yourself or others.

sources.text:
Seizures. Most seizures stop within 2 minutes. Keep your pet safe, time it, and call your vet.
Signs: Collapse, stiff or paddling legs; Jaw chomping, drooling, losing control of pee or poo; Not responding to you; Afterwards: confused, wobbly, briefly blind
What to do now:
1. Stay calm and note the time it starts.
2. Move furniture and objects away, keep them away from stairs and water, and put a towel under the head. Keep your hands away from the mouth.
3. Dim the lights and keep things quiet. Film it if you can, since it helps the vet.
4. Afterwards, keep them somewhere quiet and cool, and speak softly while they recover.
5. Call your vet after any first seizure. Go now if it lasts over 5 minutes, they have another one, they don't wake up between seizures, or they may have eaten a poison.
Don't: Putting fingers or anything else in their mouth. Pets can't swallow their tongue. Holding them down. Giving food, water or medicine until they're fully alert.
Go to a vet now.

sources.text:
Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: I accidentally put my dog's flea spot-on on my cat.
A: This can be life-threatening, so treat it as an emergency. Many dog flea and tick products contain permethrin, which cats can't break down well. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, even if she seems fine.

Signs include drooling, restlessness, twitching or trembling, wobbliness, vomiting and seizures.

- Stop her from licking the area.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Only use flea products labelled for cats, and keep cats away from newly treated dogs until the product dries.

Q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
A: Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.

Q: My cat keeps shaking her head and scratching her ears. Ear mites?
A: It could be. Ear mites are tiny parasites that live in the ear canal and are especially common in cats. Signs include:
- Head shaking
- Scratching at the ears
- Itching that can be mild or severe
- A drooping ear

Ear mites spread easily between pets, so every animal that has contact with your cat should be treated at the same time.

Other ear problems look similar, so let your vet confirm the cause and show you how to clean the ears. See a vet soon if the ear is swollen, has pus, or your cat seems to be in pain. Ask your vet for a product that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females

Q: My cat ate some leftover adobo cooked with lots of garlic and onion. Is that bad?
A: It can be. Onions, garlic and chives can upset the stomach and damage red blood cells, which can lead to anemia. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, so dishes cooked with them are risky for cats.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, especially if she ate a fair amount or you're not sure how much.

Watch for vomiting, drooling, low energy, weakness and pale gums.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what dish it was and roughly how much she ate.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Avoid sharing seasoned human food with pets.

Q: My dog got hit by a motorcycle but he's walking and seems okay. Does he still need a vet?
A: Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers

- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: Should I change my senior pet's food?
A: Maybe. Older dogs and cats have different needs:

Senior dogs:
- Usually need fewer calories, and gain weight easily
- May benefit from more fiber and good-quality protein to protect muscle

Senior cats:
- Often digest food less well, and may lose weight and muscle
- May need tasty, easy-to-digest, higher-protein food in smaller, more frequent meals

For both, aim for a healthy body shape, not too thin and not too heavy. Extra weight strains joints, while weight loss can be a sign of illness such as kidney disease.

Change foods slowly over several days. Ask your vet to check your pet's weight and muscle and suggest a diet that suits its health.

Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: How often does my adult dog need booster shots?
A: It depends on the vaccine:
- Distemper, parvovirus and adenovirus: after the puppy series and an early booster (at about 6 months or 1 year old), modern vaccines protect for years. Global guidelines advise boosting no more often than every 3 years.
- Leptospirosis: protection is shorter, so it is usually given every year.
- Rabies: some vaccines last 1 year and some 3 years, but in the Philippines the rules of the Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) require a yearly anti-rabies shot.

Your vet will make a booster plan based on your dog's age, health, lifestyle and the products used.

sources.text:
Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

Q: I accidentally put my dog's flea spot-on on my cat.
A: This can be life-threatening, so treat it as an emergency. Many dog flea and tick products contain permethrin, which cats can't break down well. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, even if she seems fine.

Signs include drooling, restlessness, twitching or trembling, wobbliness, vomiting and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the product box.
- Ask the vet on the phone whether to wash the spot first. They may tell you to use mild dish soap and plenty of water, then dry her well.
- Stop her from licking the area.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Only use flea products labelled for cats, and keep cats away from newly treated dogs until the product dries.

Q: Can I use my dog's flea medicine on my cat?
A: No. Some flea and tick products that are safe for dogs are toxic to cats.

Stay safe:
- Only use a product labeled for cats, and check that it fits your cat's age and weight
- After treating your dog, keep your cat away from him until the product is dry
- Read the label every time
- Ask your vet before using any product on a kitten, a sick, old, pregnant or nursing pet

Go to a vet right away if your pet shows drooling, shaking or trembling, wobbly walking, seizures, vomiting or unusual tiredness after a flea product. Remove a flea collar at once if it causes a reaction. Bring the package with you.

Q: My dog suddenly collapsed and isn't responding to me.
A: This needs a vet immediately. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic and leave right away.

Quick checks:
- Breathing: watch whether the chest rises and falls.
- Heartbeat: put your hand flat on the chest to feel for it.

If there's no breathing or heartbeat, ask the clinic on the phone to guide you through chest compressions. Keep going until your dog breathes on his own or the vet takes over.

On the way:
- Have someone else drive, especially if you're doing compressions.
- Lay him on a firm, flat surface and keep his head level and neck straight.
- Be careful when he wakes up, since a confused dog may bite.

sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Q: How much exercise does my old dog need?
A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

Make home easier:
- Non-slip rugs or yoga mats on smooth floors
- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

If your dog limps, stops often or is stiff after walks, he may be in pain. Ask your vet for a check and an exercise plan.

Q: How do I know if my old dog has arthritis?
A: Arthritis (joint wear and pain) is common in older dogs. Look for:
- Stiffness, especially after resting
- Limping or a changed way of walking
- Trouble with stairs, jumping into the car or onto the sofa, or getting up
- Less interest in walks or play
- Thinner leg muscles
- Grumpiness or snapping when touched

What helps:
- Keep your dog at a healthy weight
- Gentle, regular exercise like leash walks
- Non-slip rugs and ramps at home

See your vet for a proper diagnosis and pain plan. Don't give any pain medicine, including human medicine, without your vet's advice.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: How can I tell if my pet's problem is a real emergency or can wait?
A: An emergency is any sudden, serious problem. If you're unsure, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. They can tell you whether to come in.

Go immediately if your pet:
- Has trouble breathing, breathes with the mouth open (cats), or has blue or very pale gums
- Is bleeding heavily
- Collapses, is unresponsive, or has a seizure
- Ate something poisonous
- Was hit by a vehicle or fell, even if they seem fine
- Is straining to pee with nothing coming out (especially male cats)
- Has a swollen belly and keeps retching (dogs)
- Suddenly acts very differently from normal

Save your vet's number and the nearest 24-hour clinic in your phone today, and know the route.

Q: My male cat keeps crying in the litter box and licking his private area. Can it wait until tomorrow?
A: Please don't wait. A male cat that strains and passes little or no urine may have a blocked urethra. This is an absolute emergency. When urine can't get out, toxins build up quickly, and a blocked cat can die in less than a day or two.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Other signs include blood in the urine, peeing outside the box, frequent trips to the box, and becoming more and more distressed.

On the way:
- Place him gently in a carrier and don't squeeze his belly.
- Keep him calm and quiet.
- Tell the clinic it's a male cat who can't pee, so they can be ready.

Q: My male cat keeps going to the litter box but nothing comes out.
A: This can be a blocked bladder, which is an emergency in male cats. Take him to a vet now. A blockage can become life-threatening within a day.

Other signs include crying in the litter box, licking his genitals, vomiting, or hiding. Don't wait to see if it passes, and don't press on his belly. The vet can check his bladder and relieve the blockage.

sources.label: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals
sources.text:
Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Overview
There are many health benefits of owning a pet. They can increase opportunities to exercise, get outside, and socialize. Regular walking or playing with pets can decrease blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and triglyceride levels. Pets can help manage loneliness and depression by providing companionship. Studies have shown that the bond between people and their pets is linked to several health benefits, including: - Decreased blood pressure, cholesterol and triglyceride (fat) levels, feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. - Increased opportunities for exercise and outdoor activities, better cognitive function in older adults, and more opportunities to socialize. However, pets can sometimes carry harmful germs that can make us sick even when the pet appears healthy. The diseases people get from animals are called zoonotic diseases. Below are some tips to help you and your family stay healthy while enjoying pets.

messages.content: body condition score for dogs and cats

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

sources.label: FurFriends checked answer
sources.text:
Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Diseases spread by mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks
Mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks are common pests of stray animals and can be a problem immediately after a disaster. Their bites irritate the skin and can also spread a variety of diseases harmful to both people and animals. These include Lyme disease and West Nile virus. To help prevent illnesses associated with mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks: - Keep your pet away from wildlife and stray animals. - Provide your pet with regular preventative care. Talk to your pet's veterinarian about regular treatment for fleas, ticks, and parasites prevention.

sources.text:
CPR. Only for a pet who is unconscious, not breathing and has no heartbeat. Get someone to drive to the vet while you work.
Signs: Doesn't respond when you call or touch them; No chest movement for 10 seconds; No heartbeat on the left side of the chest, just behind the elbow
What to do now:
1. Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Put flat-chested breeds like Bulldogs on their back.
2. Cats and small dogs: wrap one hand around the chest just behind the elbows and squeeze. Larger dogs: stack both hands on the widest part of the chest. On their back: press on the breastbone.
3. Push hard and fast: a third to a half of the chest's width, 100â€“120 times a minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest come all the way back up.
4. After 30 compressions, close the mouth, straighten the neck and give 2 quick breaths into the nose, watching the chest rise.
5. Keep going 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Check for breathing and a heartbeat every 2 minutes, and keep going on the way to the vet.
Don't: CPR on a pet who is breathing or has a heartbeat. It can hurt them.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog ate a few slices of raisin bread but he seems totally fine.
A: Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

Q: My dog ate a handful of macadamia nuts from a cookie tin.
A: Macadamia nuts can make dogs sick, usually within 12 hours. Signs include weakness, vomiting, wobbling, tremors, fever and low energy. Most dogs get better within 1 to 3 days, but call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Cookies and nut mixes can also contain chocolate or raisins, which are more dangerous, so tell the vet everything that was in the tin.

Before you go:
- Bring the packaging and estimate how much he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and comfortable, and note any vomiting or shaking.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog licked toilet bowl cleaner and my cat stepped in spilled bleach. What do I do?
A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Cats — What to do if you are bitten or scratched by a cat
If you are bitten or scratched by a cat, you should: Wash wounds with warm soapy water immediately. Seek medical attention if: - You don't know if the cat has been vaccinated against rabies. - The cat appears sick. - The wound is serious. - The wound becomes red, painful, warm or swollen. - It has been more than 5 years since your last tetanus shot. Report the bite to animal control or your local health department if the bite is unprovoked and - The cat is a stray, or - You are unsure if the cat has been vaccinated against rabies. Cat bites carry the risk of spreading rabies to humans. Ensure the cat is seen by a veterinarian if it becomes sick or dies shortly after the bite. Report the bite by contacting your local health department.

Q: My dog walked through insecticide our neighbor sprayed and now he's drooling and shaking.
A: This could be insecticide poisoning, which can get serious fast. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs from many bug sprays, such as organophosphates and carbamates, include heavy drooling, tiny pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, peeing a lot, trembling, weakness, trouble breathing and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- If he's breathing well and it won't delay you, wear gloves and gently wash his paws and coat with mild dish soap and lots of water. Don't scrub with a brush.
- If he's struggling to breathe, skip the bath and go straight away.
- Bring the product label, or ask the neighbor what was used.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't rub oil on him.

Keep pets off sprayed areas until they are dry.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Choking
sources.text:
Choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.
Signs: Pawing at the mouth, gagging or retching; Panic, struggling to breathe; Blue or pale gums; Collapse
What to do now:
1. Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
2. Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
3. If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
4. For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
5. Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
6. Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.
Don't: Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper. Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog was panting really hard after our walk in the heat and now he collapsed. What do I do?
A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

sources.label: FurFriends checked answer
sources.text:
Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

messages.content: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?

Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: How much exercise does my old dog need?
A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

Make home easier:
- Non-slip rugs or yoga mats on smooth floors
- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

If your dog limps, stops often or is stiff after walks, he may be in pain. Ask your vet for a check and an exercise plan.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Eye injuries. Eyes get worse fast. Flat-faced breeds like Shih Tzus and Pugs are prone to eye injuries, and an eye can even pop out.
Signs: Squinting, an eye held shut, pawing at it; Redness, tearing, cloudiness; Something stuck in the eye; An eye bulging out of its socket
What to do now:
1. Stop them rubbing it. Use a cone collar or hold their paws.
2. Chemicals: flush the eye with sterile saline or clean, lukewarm water for 10â€“15 minutes.
3. Eye out of its socket: keep it moist with a clean cloth soaked in saline and go straight away.
4. Go to the vet the same day for any eye injury.
Don't: Removing something stuck in the eye. Pushing a bulging eye back in. Human eye drops or ointments.
Go to a vet now.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Choking
sources.text:
Choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.
Signs: Pawing at the mouth, gagging or retching; Panic, struggling to breathe; Blue or pale gums; Collapse
What to do now:
1. Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
2. Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
3. If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
4. For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
5. Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
6. Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.
Don't: Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper. Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My cat keeps shaking her head and scratching her ears. Ear mites?
A: It could be. Ear mites are tiny parasites that live in the ear canal and are especially common in cats. Signs include:
- Head shaking
- Scratching at the ears
- Itching that can be mild or severe
- A drooping ear

Ear mites spread easily between pets, so every animal that has contact with your cat should be treated at the same time.

Other ear problems look similar, so let your vet confirm the cause and show you how to clean the ears. See a vet soon if the ear is swollen, has pus, or your cat seems to be in pain. Ask your vet for a product that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: How often should I deworm my kitten?
A: Kittens often get roundworms from their mother's milk, so deworming starts early.

Parasite experts (CAPC) advise:
- Start at 2 weeks old
- Repeat every 2 weeks until your kitten starts a monthly year-round parasite preventive
- If a monthly preventive isn't used: every 2 weeks until 2 months old, then monthly until 6 months, then every 3 months
- Have the kitten's poop checked by the vet several times in the first year

Ask your vet for a product that suits your kitten's weight and age, and use only products made for cats.

Q: Should I change my senior pet's food?
A: Maybe. Older dogs and cats have different needs:

Senior dogs:
- Usually need fewer calories, and gain weight easily
- May benefit from more fiber and good-quality protein to protect muscle

Senior cats:
- Often digest food less well, and may lose weight and muscle
- May need tasty, easy-to-digest, higher-protein food in smaller, more frequent meals

For both, aim for a healthy body shape, not too thin and not too heavy. Extra weight strains joints, while weight loss can be a sign of illness such as kidney disease.

Change foods slowly over several days. Ask your vet to check your pet's weight and muscle and suggest a diet that suits its health.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: My dog licked toilet bowl cleaner and my cat stepped in spilled bleach. What do I do?
A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners, as this makes a toxic gas.

Q: My senior dog seems confused and paces at night. What's wrong?
A: This can be a sign of cognitive dysfunction, a condition like dementia in people. It affects about 14 to 22% of dogs over 8 years old. Signs include:
- Getting lost or stuck in corners at home
- Sleeping more in the day and restless at night
- Less interest in family members
- Toilet accidents in the house
- Pacing, anxiety or barking for no clear reason

Cats can get it too, and often meow more.

Pain, vision loss and other illnesses can cause similar changes, so see your vet for a full check. Treatment works best when started early. Gentle exercise, new toys and simple games can help keep your pet's mind active.

A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash

- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Q: My dog drank some beer someone left on the table during our party.
A: Alcohol is absorbed quickly and can be dangerous for pets. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Signs include vomiting, diarrhea, wobbling, sleepiness, trouble breathing and tremors, and in severe cases coma or death.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what drink it was and roughly how much he had.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't give coffee or anything else to "sober him up". Caffeine is also toxic to pets.

On the way, keep him calm and watch his breathing.

Raw bread dough with yeast can also make alcohol inside the stomach, so keep both drinks and dough out of reach.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: My dog got hit by a motorcycle but he's walking and seems okay. Does he still need a vet?
A: Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

sources.text:
Bleeding & wounds. Most bleeding stops with firm, steady pressure. Bite wounds can look small but often get infected.
Signs: Bleeding that spurts or won't stop; A deep or gaping wound, or one on the chest or belly; Puncture wounds from another animal's bite; Pale gums, weakness (blood loss)
What to do now:
1. If they're in pain, use a soft muzzle or towel so they don't bite. Skip this if they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
2. Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze for at least 5 minutes. Don't lift it to check.
3. If blood soaks through, add more layers on top. Don't remove the first one.
4. Once it stops, wrap it snugly but not tight. You should fit two fingers under the bandage.
5. Go to the vet for anything deeper than a scrape, all bite wounds, and any bleeding that won't stop.
Don't: Tourniquets, unless you're trained. They can kill the limb. Hydrogen peroxide or alcohol in the wound. They damage tissue. Pulling out something stuck in the wound.
Go to a vet now.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

sources.text:
Vomiting & diarrhea. One episode in a bright, adult pet is often minor. Call your vet for advice and watch closely for the warning signs below.
Signs: Go now: repeated vomiting, or they can't keep water down; Go now: blood in the vomit or stool, or black, tarry stool; Go now: swollen or painful belly, weakness or collapse; Go now: a puppy or kitten, or an unvaccinated young dog (parvovirus risk); Go now: may have swallowed a toy, bone or poison
What to do now:
1. Call your vet and describe what you've seen. A photo helps.
2. Offer small amounts of water often.
3. If your vet agrees, feed small portions of bland food, like plain boiled chicken and rice for dogs.
4. Keep a sick puppy away from other dogs and disinfect the area. Parvovirus spreads easily.
Don't: Human anti-diarrhea or stomach medicines. Some are toxic to cats and some dogs. Withholding food from a cat for more than a day. It can cause liver disease.
Call your vet for advice.
